newsitem.title: USA: U.S. smoke trial judge threatens to issue gag order.
newsitem.headline: U.S. smoke trial judge threatens to issue gag order.

text.p: The judge in a landmark $5 billion secondhand-smoke trial on Tuesday accused rival lawyers of ignoring his directives against talking to reporters and threatened to slap a gag order on them.
"I don't want any comment. If you want me to issue a gag order, I will," Judge Robert Kaye told lawyers for both sides before tobacco industry representatives opened defence arguments.

In an unprecedented case against seven tobacco companies and two industry groups, thousands of airline flight attendants are seeking damages for health problems they say were caused by passengers' smoke on airliners.
Kaye already has barred access to documents and forbidden the publication of jurors' names out of fear their verdict might be influenced by news coverage.

The judge issued his directive after Susan Rosenblatt, one of the lawyers pressing the case, said in court that an RJ Reynolds Tobacco executive had violated the judge's pre-trial directives during a courthouse press briefing Monday.

She said Dan Donohue, an executive vice president with Reynolds, had hurt the class action suit by suggesting that fewer than 100 non-smoking flight attendants had tobacco-related diseases of the sort attributed in the lawsuit to secondhand smoke.
"We don't want the jury thinking we are talking about a few hundred people," Rosenblatt said.
Rosenblatt said nearly 9,000 flight attendants had registered with her and her co-counsel, husband Stanley Rosenblatt, and thousands more had requested information about the case.
She said the members of the class -- defined as non-smoking flight attendants with such ailments as lung cancer who worked before 1988 -- could be as high as 100,000.

Kaye ruled last week that the number of flight attendants in the class action, the first ever against the tobacco industry to come to trial in the United States, should not be mentioned during the trial.
Tobacco company lawyers said Donohue was working as a corporate spokesman and was not part of the legal team fighting the class action.
They also accused Stanley Rosenblatt of giving a brief interview to at least one newspaper on Monday.
Kaye said he would issue a formal order barring lawyers, witnesses and plaintiffs from talking to reporters under pain of court punishment if his directives were ignored again.
"I don't want this jury to be infected by media comment," Kaye said.
When the six-member jury came into the courtroom to hear opening arguments by tobacco lawyers on Tuesday, Kaye repeated instructions to them to avoid reading or watching news reports about the trial.

One juror told Kaye he had just learned that a friend had once worked as a flight attendant, but the judge, after being reassured by the juror that the relationship would not affect his verdict, kept the man on the jury.
Last week Kaye excused one juror and two alternate jurors just days after they were selected.

David Hardy, a lawyer for defendants Philip Morris Inc. and Lorrillard, said in opening arguments that the dangers of secondhand smoke were trivial and that inhaling smoke from other people's cigarettes was in no way similar to smoking itself.
"The amount of (secondhand) smoke anyone is exposed to is so tiny it's almost meaningless," Hardy said.

Hardy said Stanley Rosenblatt, who spoke to the jury on Monday, will not be able to prove his claims that secondhand smoke causes disease among non-smokers and the seven companies and two trade groups fighting the lawsuit conspired from the 1950s until now to hide the dangers of cigarettes.
"What he won't tell you is that the (secondhand) smoke is diluted hundreds of times by the air," Hardy said.
Testimoney in the trial of the case, Norma Broin et al vs Philip Morris et al, is scheduled to begin on Wednesday.
